title: Greeting the mosque
hookLine: two short units on arriving, a greeting for the house (Bukhari)

cards: This week you've walked all the way into a mosque. Shoes off, right foot in, asking for the doors of mercy. Washed at the low taps.
Found the niche that shows the way, and the steps for the sermon. Stood in a row with no gaps. Now you're inside, there's a carpet, and you'd like to sit down.
Plenty of places have a small hello before you settle in: a bow at the edge of a judo mat, a nod to the room before a meeting starts. A mosque has its own. Today: greeting the mosque.

teach.b: It's called tahiyyat al-masjid, the greeting of the mosque. Tahiyyah means a greeting, the same word used for the greetings in the sitting of the prayer.
Bukhari and Muslim report, from the companion Abu Qatadah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: when one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before he sits down.
Two short units of prayer: standing, bowing, prostrating, twice, then the peace to both sides. A minute or two, then you sit. A story in Sahih Muslim shows how seriously he meant it.

teach.h: SULAYK, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SERMON.
teach.b: One Friday, while the Prophet was giving the sermon, a man named Sulayk came in and sat straight down. The Prophet stopped and asked him: did you pray two rak'ahs? He said no.
The Prophet told him: stand, and pray two, and keep them short. In the middle of the sermon. Scholars have worked out the details, and they don't all agree.
They generally hold that if the congregational prayer is already starting, joining it is enough.

teach.h: THE SCHOOLS DIFFER ON THE DETAILS.
teach.b: The Hanafi and Maliki schools say not to pray it once the Friday sermon has begun, reading the Sulayk story as a special case; the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools say to pray it, briefly.
They also differ about the times of day when voluntary prayer is usually avoided. Why greet a building? Not because the walls are holy, but because of who the house is for.
Some scholars explain it as greeting the Lord of the house before you greet anyone in it.

teach.h: YOUR FIRST ACT INSIDE IS A BOW.
teach.b: You come in from traffic and email, and your first act inside isn't to check your phone. It's to bow.

how: On entering a mosque, Muslims are taught to pray two short rak'ahs before sitting, called tahiyyat al-masjid; if the congregational prayer is starting, they join it instead, and schools differ on praying it during the Friday sermon.

o: two short prayer units on arriving, before you sit
saying salaam to everyone already in the hall
a coin dropped in the charity box by the entrance

games.q: what's inside the greeting of the mosque — tap the pairs.

s: the Prophet ﷺ told Sulayk to pray two rak'ahs in the middle of the sermon
stand, pray two, and keep them short (Muslim).
all the schools agree on praying it during the Friday sermon
Hanafis and Malikis say not to once the sermon starts; Shafi'is and Hanbalis say to pray it briefly.
the greeting means the mosque's walls are holy
some scholars explain it as greeting the Lord of the house, not the building.

games.q: you walk into the mosque an hour before the prayer. there's a soft carpet, and you're tired. what does the hadith say to do first?
o: sit down right away and rest
wait standing until the prayer starts
games.why: when one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before he sits (Bukhari, Muslim). then rest.

practice: If you pray, you can stand now and pray two short rak'ahs, as a greeting for wherever you are. If you don't, plan a visit instead: which mosque, which day; some mosques hold open days, and it's fine to call ahead.
Either way, finish by sitting still and picturing the walk in: shoes off, right foot first, water, the niche, the rows, and your first act inside a greeting.

wordCard.voice: Tahiyyat al-masjid. The greeting of the mosque: two short units of prayer on arriving, before you sit down. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the greeting of the mosque, two short units of prayer on arriving.

carryVoice: Your line: greet the house. Not the walls, but the one the house is for. Day one hundred forty-two, done.
